strengths: The manuscript identifies a useful gap in RVOS: expressions whose resolution depends on relationships between multiple entities. InterRVOS-8K is substantial in nominal scale, containing 8,738 videos, 35,247 objects, 127,314 expressions, and 17,682 actor-target interactions. The four-stage annotation pipeline and full prompts are documented in considerable detail.

There is encouraging evidence that the data can transfer beyond the proposed benchmark. With the same Sa2VA baseline, InterRVOS-5K obtains zero-shot J&F scores of 41.8 on MeViS-valid, 61.8 on Ref-Youtube-VOS, and 67.1 on Ref-DAVIS, compared with 32.8, 54.2, and 62.1 for Ref-SAV training.

The proposed model is computationally pragmatic, fine-tuning only LoRA modules and the SAM2 decoder. On the authors' benchmark, ReVIOSa-1B improves overall J&F from 53.8 for Sa2VA-1B to 59.7, while the reported ablation favors joint actor-target training over single-token and independently supervised variants.
weaknesses: The central semantic formulation is internally inconsistent. The paper alternates between 'actor' meaning the causal initiator and meaning the grammatical/referred subject. For example, in 'child getting styled by adult,' the child is shown as [SEG_ACT] even though the adult performs the action. This contradicts the claimed actor-target semantics and the Stage-4 prompt, which defines the subject as the performer. Consequently, it is unclear what roles the tokens and annotations consistently represent.

The automatically generated dataset receives no reported human validation. There is no audited sample, correctness rate, inter-annotator agreement, or breakdown of errors in interaction detection, directionality, referential uniqueness, or caption-mask correspondence. Visible examples already contain malformed or semantically weak captions such as 'Person holding for black and brown dog and medium-sized dog' and 'person handing to person.' Thus, scale does not establish annotation quality, and the test labels are not an independent ground truth because they are generated through the same pipeline as the training annotations.

A crucial part of dataset construction is missing: the manuscript does not explain how dense segmentation mask tracks are obtained or validated. It states that the dataset is built on VidOR, but VidOR is ordinarily described through tracked boxes and visual-relation annotations; the paper neither documents a box-to-mask procedure nor reports mask quality. It also inconsistently cites Thomee et al.'s YFCC100M paper as VidOR in Section 3. This omission directly affects the validity and reproducibility of the segmentation benchmark.

The actor-target evaluation protocol is inadequately defined. The paper says it applies standard RVOS evaluation to interaction samples forming expression pairs, but does not specify whether J and F average both simultaneously predicted masks, score only the referred mask, or require correct role assignment as a pair. No actor-versus-target scores, pair-level success metric, or role-confusion analysis is provided. Therefore, Tables 5 and 6 do not convincingly substantiate the central claim of correct joint role-aware segmentation.

Most headline evidence is measured on the authors' automatically generated and deliberately interaction-enriched evaluation set. This favors models trained on matching captions and annotation artifacts. The standard-benchmark zero-shot results support the usefulness of the data, but ReVIOSa itself is worse than the Sa2VA baseline on three of four reported conventional evaluations, including Ref-Youtube-VOS and Ref-DAVIS, weakening claims of broadly improved video understanding.

Comparison conditions are not sufficiently specified. Table 5 does not clearly state the training data and identical optimization conditions used for every competing method, while the construction and sampling of the 2K/5K subsets are omitted. Results are reported from apparently single runs without variance. These issues make architectural and data-quality conclusions difficult to separate from training-budget or sampling effects.

The architectural novelty is limited to introducing two segmentation tokens and joint supervision on top of InternVL, Sa2VA-style grounding, and SAM2. The paper gives no formal model or loss equations and omits essential implementation details such as optimizer, learning rate, frame sampling, input resolution, inference procedure, and loss weights. The displayed project-page URL is blank, and no code, data-access, licensing, or release information is supplied.

Overall, the task direction and transfer results are worthwhile, but the unresolved role-definition contradiction, absent validation of automatically generated language and masks, and underdefined central evaluation prevent the reported numbers from convincingly supporting the paper's main claims. These are material scientific issues rather than presentation refinements, so the balance favors rejection.
